newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany-Asia air cargo rates steady, volumes rise.
newsitem.headline: Germany-Asia air cargo rates steady, volumes rise.

text.p: Air cargo rates from Germany to Asian and Middle East destinations are generally holding steady at present, a Reuters survey shows.
Strong growth in German exports this spring is mostly matching an increase in freight capacity to several major cargo gateways, industry sources said.
But market rates to Seoul, Hong Kong and South-east Asia are influenced by discounting as an imbalance between capacity and demand follows a general round of price hikes in March.

Airlines have followed the lead of Lufthansa Cargo by dropping their cargo fuel surcharge of 15 pfennigs per kg from mid-April, but there are few signs of rate rises in order to keep prices at the higher level.

The German market has now picked up after a slow start to the year with overall tonnage rising 7.5 percent in March and showing a 5.8 percent increase in the first quarter of 1997, the German airports association ADV said.
At Frankfurt, the country's air cargo gateway, total air cargo rose 7.9 percent in March and grew 5.1 percent in the first quarter.

But Lufthansa Cargo, which flies a high proportion of its global freight tonnage via Frankfurt, saw a 4.1 percent fall in its European operations, including Germany, to 179,300 tonnes in the first quarter.
A Lufthansa Cargo source said the airline expected a reasonably strong May although no major growth was likely.

The Chinese market looks set for steady growth over the coming few months and several airlines including Lufthansa, Swissair and China Eastern have all increased rates recently, market observers said.
The Lufthansa Cargo source said that volumes to China were slightly down on last year at the start of 1997 but had picked up since March.

Frank Wortmann, managing director of Penta Shipping, sales agent for Air China, said: "The market is very good at the moment. We had a very strong April, May is looking good and we are booked out for June.
"Rates are stable apart from some increases to the provinces," he added.
The air cargo boom at end-1996 where whole machines were flown into China to beat higher import duties was now being followed by the spare parts market, Wortmann pointed out.
Air China had introduced ex-Germany +5,000kg rates for the first time which were about 30 pfennigs lower than the standard +1,000kg rates, he added.
Air China operates a weekly Boeing 747-200F joint venture with Lufthansa Cargo, plus twice-weekly 747-400 combi and twice-weekly 747-400 passenger flights between Beijing, Shanghai and Frankfurt.
Fast-growing rival China Eastern Airlines raised ex-Germany air cargo rates by five percent from April 1 due to strong demand and limited capacity.

The airline's Germany cargo sales manager, Jie Xu, said: "Shipments are coming regularly and with a rates increase we can make more profits. Since last November when we added the second flight, business has improved a lot."
Xu said he expected the market for Shanghai and other Chinese cities to grow steadily.
China Eastern flies twice-weekly Munich to Shanghai via Beijing with Airbus A340 aircraft with a maximum freight capacity of nine tonnes.

The sales manager of an Asian carrier added: "I expect tremendous increase in freight particularly because of the Chinese takeover of Hong Kong. The Chinese market will be one of the biggest in the Far East for freight from all parts of the world."
But he warned: "The Far East is still under a strong boom. But if everyone starts to fly there then there will be over-capacity like the transatlantic market and that could affect yields."
Heiner Sass, central Europe cargo director of Martinair, said he was very pleased with German bookings for the carrier's new weekly Amsterdam-Guangzhou 747-200 freighter service after a slow start.
"Bookings for Guangzhou are good and we are very happy that it has developed so well. We are very optimistic that demand will develop gradually in the future," he said.
But rates to Hong Kong and Taiwan were currently under pressure with more ad-hoc rates for Hong Kong due to the large capacity in the market, he added.
Lufthansa and Cathay Pacific, which operate the only direct Germany-Hong Kong services, have now added an 11th weekly joint B747-200F service at a time of traditionally low demand, observers said.

Martinair's Sass noted that demand for Taipei appeared to have fallen slightly due to less project business and the airline, which flies a weekly B747-200F to Taiwan, had reduced capacity in favour of China.
Market rates to Asia were otherwise generally stable and Martinair, which dropped its ex-German air cargo fuel surcharge in mid-April, did not plan a rates rise until the autumn, he added.
Ex-Frankfurt rates to Seoul have dropped in recent weeks as demand has fallen due to a slowdown in exports and sluggish foreign investment, observers said.
But an optimistic Lufthansa Cargo source said: "January and February were down but there was a recovery in March. It looks as though Seoul is recovering."
New capacity will come on to the market in late May with the start of Asiana's twice-weekly, 35-tonne capacity 747 Combi flight to Frankfurt.
The airline's Germany cargo traffic supervisor, Sasa Kantar, said: "Demand is certainly there. There have already been enquiries from forwarders."
Asiana expected forwarders to try out the new service for some time before committing themselves for a longer period, he added.
The manager of one Asian airline manager said that German exports to Japan had now tailed off slightly following a February boom prompted by Japan's the March 1 consumption tax rise on imports.
But Lufthansa Cargo said volumes for Japan were stable and rates were recovering from a drop earlier in the year.
Thai Airways' Germany cargo manager, Guillermo Valencia, noted: "There is very good demand for Japan at the moment."
The south-east Asian market appears to be growing steadily at present but without any spectacular boom, industry figures said.
The Lufthansa Cargo source said freight volumes were slightly down to south-east Asia but still acceptable although load factors could be better to Bangkok.
Thai manager Guillermo Valencia added: "There has been a slight downturn in April bookings and business is dragging a little."
Thai was having to react with special deals and more shipments were being sold at ad-hoc rates, he disclosed.
Competition to Malaysia has now hotted up with the start of a third weekly Lufthansa 747 passenger flight to Kuala Lumpur, sources said.
But MAS has dropped a planned rates hike of 20 percent after complaints by German forwarders of poor handling standards at Kuala Lumpur airport.
The problems were generated by insufficient handling space and high staff turnover, industry sources said.
An MAS spokesman said rates would probably now be held stable through 1997 until the new Sepang international airport opened with larger cargo facilities next year.
Manila is starting to emerge as an interesting air cargo market from Germany with telecommunications equipment as the main item for shipment, sources said.
A Philippines Airlines cargo spokesman said: "With our limited capacity on six passenger flights a week we have more than enough cargo on our lower lower decks."
The airline gave priority to Manila freight due to higher yields and did not accept much transhipment freight for Hong Kong or Japan, he added.
Rates to India are now holding steady at higher levels after demand picked up over the last couple of months, industry sources said.
Air India will increase ex-Germany air cargo rates by 10 percent from June 1 as the launch of combi and freighter services more than triple its weekly capacity to 100 tonnes from 30 tonnes.

From June 1, the carrier will fly 747-300 combi flights twice-weekly to Paris and weekly to Amsterdam with Frankfurt stopovers and will start a weekly 747-200 freighter from Paris via Frankfurt to India on July 1.
Germany cargo sales manager, Ruediger Brasche, said: "Now with this higher capacity back in the market we must see how the market reacts. The hour of truth will come in the next few weeks."
A Lufthansa Cargo source said: "Rates to India have remained constant. Since Air India changed its flight schedule very strongly because of the Haj, demand has been stronger."
But low prices offered by Polar Air Cargo on its flights from Europe to India were putting strong pressure on Delhi rates which tend to be lower than prices for Bombay, the source added.
Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) has kept ex-Germany rates stable this spring after dropping its cargo fuel surcharge on April 21.
Ashfaq Maher, PIA cargo manager for Germany and Austria, said: "The Pakistan market is growing, mostly for exports to Europe. The market is going well but there is more competition there."
PIA has three weekly 707F flights, twice-weekly 747 combi services and a weekly A310 passenger flight between Pakistan and Germany.
New capacity will come on to the Pakistan market from May 26 with the launch of a weekly, 40-tonne capacity 707F flight between Lahore and Ostend by Pakistan cargo airline Shaheen Air Cargo.
Mohammad Shamim, the airline's western Europe general manager, said: "Pakistan is opening up and PIA cannot offer enough capacity, which is why it is the right time to start this service.
"Lahore is the main freight hub in Pakistan and flights will be full from Pakistan. It is a question of how much we can fly back (from Europe)," he added.
The Lahore market was currently generating about 400 tonnes of export air cargo a week, mostly textiles and leather goods, Shamim said.

Prices to the Middle East remain under pressure with a large amount of ad-hoc offers due to a general increase in capacity, sources indicated. --Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel +44 171 542 7706 Fax+5017
